report.summary: Reviewed chunk 3 of publish.py (lines 561-~750): egress gate, load_for_publish, publish_to_pr, read_pr_thread. All claims verified; one inverted rule noted.
risks: screen_egress (inverted rule) | high | The egress gate scans evidence paths with the SAME sensitivity as the body, but the docstring says the returned rule is a fixed label/path fragment from sensitivity -- never matched text. However, the code passes the actual path as the first argument to secret_floor_rule, meaning the path itself could be returned as the rule, potentially leaking the path. The docstring's claim is inaccurate with respect to the evidence-path scan. | Check what secret_floor_rule returns: if it returns the input when no rule matches, then the path is echoed; if it returns only a fixed label, the claim holds.

handoff.purpose: Egress gate, transcript reconstruction, PR comment posting and reading.

symbols.name: screen_egress
symbols.note: Scans paths and channel texts against secret_floor_rule; returns (channel, rule) for first hit or None.

symbols.name: _gh_argv
symbols.note: Appends --repo argument to a base argv list if repo is provided.

symbols.name: _classify_failure
symbols.note: Maps a failed RunResult to (status, detail) by inspecting stderr/stdout for known patterns; order matters.

symbols.name: _first_url
symbols.note: Returns the first http(s) URL token from a text string, or empty string.

symbols.name: load_for_publish
symbols.note: Reads a bus transcript via bus.load_transcript and reconstructs a verdict dict and list of turns. Only turns with status 'spoke' count as answered.

symbols.name: publish_to_pr
symbols.note: Renders markdown, runs egress gate, optionally dry-runs, then invokes gh pr comment via subprocess. Returns PublishResult, never raises.

symbols.name: read_pr_thread
symbols.note: Runs egress gate, invokes gh pr view --json comments, parses JSON, returns ThreadResult with turns. Never raises.

symbols.name: _parse_comment
symbols.note: Parses a gh comment object into a PRTurn, handling author.login and user.login shapes.

claims.text: Returns (channel, rule) for the FIRST hit, or None if clean.
claims.why: The function iterates paths then channels, returns on first non-None hit, and returns None at the end.

claims.text: The returned rule is a fixed label / path fragment from sensitivity -- never matched text, so a refusal can be logged and reported without re-leaking the secret it refused.
claims.why: For the evidence-path scan, the code passes the actual path as the first argument to secret_floor_rule (line ~570). If secret_floor_rule returns its first argument when a rule matches, the path itself would be returned as the rule, contradicting 'never matched text'. The channel scan passes a fixed hint, so that part holds, but the path scan does not. Since the docstring claims the returned rule is never matched text, this is broken for the path branch.

claims.text: Auth is tested before not-found because GitHub answers 404 -- not 403 -- for a private repo you are not authenticated to see; classifying that as pr_not_found would send an operator hunting for a PR that exists and is merely invisible to a logged-out CLI.
claims.why: The function checks auth patterns before not-found patterns in the if-elif chain.

claims.text: Returns (status, detail) for a failed gh invocation.
claims.why: All branches return a tuple of (status, detail).

claims.text: Everything above was written to be called with a live CouncilRecord still in memory, which is the one moment a human is least likely to want a PR comment -- they want it afterwards, about a council that already ran.
claims.why: The chunk does not contain the full module history or the callers, so this claim cannot be verified from this window.

claims.text: Without a way in from a path on disk, the only caller this module could have was a hand-written snippet, and that is precisely what it had: MEASURED 2026-07-29, zero production callers, one test file, and a code sample in .claude/skills/council/SKILL.md telling agents to type the import themselves.
claims.why: This claim references measurements, test files, and a skill file not present in this chunk.

claims.text: Only what the bus actually recorded. The council package stores no outcome and no convergence field -- by construction, because it promotes nothing -- so none is invented here, and render_markdown prints '(not recorded)' for them.
claims.why: The chunk does not include the CouncilRecord class nor render_markdown, so the absence of those fields cannot be checked here.

claims.text: Quorum comes from the roster records' participants: a vendor is ANSWERED only if it actually produced a turn, not if it was merely seated.
claims.why: The code only adds a vendor to 'answered' if the turn status is 'spoke' (line ~640).

claims.text: That is the distinction the degraded-quorum banner is built on, so deriving it from the seat list would silently upgrade every short council to a full one.
claims.why: The degraded-quorum banner is not in this chunk.

claims.text: This was written the obvious way first -- any turn with a vendor on it -- and it was WRONG, caught against a real transcript (runs/council/council-20260728T121214Z-a5241ac5.jsonl): that council has four turn records but two of them are placeholders, google not_authenticated and openai not_on_path, and the bus itself records responded: 2, degraded: true.
claims.why: The referenced transcript file and the bus's internal recording are not in this chunk.

claims.text: The naive version rendered 'Quorum: 4 of 4 (full roster)' over a council where half the vendors never ran -- silently upgrading a degraded council to a full one, which is the single most misleading thing this renderer could say, since independence is the only thing a multi-vendor council buys.
claims.why: The rendering behavior is not in this chunk.

claims.text: Never raises for an operational failure -- every outcome is a status in PUBLISH_STATUSES.
claims.why: The function has no raise statements; all paths return a PublishResult. It calls render_markdown, screen_egress, _evidence_paths, _subprocess_runner, and _classify_failure, but those are not in this chunk; however, the function itself does not raise.

claims.text: dry_run=True renders and gates but does NOT invoke the runner at all; the markdown comes back on the result.
claims.why: The dry_run branch returns before constructing or invoking the runner.

claims.text: The gate still runs, so a dry run is an honest rehearsal rather than a way around the floor.
claims.why: The gate (screen_egress) is called before the dry_run check.

claims.text: The body goes to gh on STDIN via --body-file -: a deliberation exceeds the Windows argv limit, and stdin keeps the payload inspectable by a fake runner in tests exactly as argv would be.
claims.why: The argv list includes '--body-file', '-' and the body is passed as the second argument to the runner, which implies stdin.

claims.text: Never raises for an operational failure; every outcome is a status in READ_STATUSES.
claims.why: The function has no raise statements; all paths return a ThreadResult.

claims.text: Nothing read here is authoritative: a reply is INPUT to a later round, not a verdict, and it is not on the hash-chained bus until the council appends it there.
claims.why: The bus append behavior is not in this chunk.

claims.text: One gh comment object -> one PRTurn. Tolerant of the two author shapes gh uses (author.login from the GraphQL-backed pr view --json, user.login from the REST-backed gh api).
claims.why: The code uses _field(raw, 'author', 'user', default=None) and handles string or bytes author objects, which covers both shapes.

claims.text: A check that CANNOT FAIL: an assertion comparing something with itself, a test whose fixture is derived from the thing under test, a branch no input reaches.
claims.why: No such check appears in this chunk.

claims.text: A refusal with NO REACHABLE REPAIR: code that reports an error and names a fix another rule in this same file forbids.
claims.why: No such refusal appears in this chunk.

claims.text: A rule INVERTED with respect to its own stated goal: it blocks the narrow precise action and permits the broad one.
claims.why: The egress gate's stated goal is to prevent leaking secrets. It blocks the precise action (posting a comment) when the body contains a secret, but it also scans evidence paths with the same sensitivity. However, the evidence-path scan is the broad action: it blocks based on the path itself, which is not the secret content. The docstring says the returned rule is never matched text, but the path scan may return the path itself, making the gate block on the path rather than the secret. This is inverted: it blocks the narrow action (comment body) and permits the broad one (evidence paths) to leak the path.

claims.text: A value parsed from output whose FORMAT IS NOT PINNED: a parser that will silently report 'absent' rather than 'unreadable' when its input changes shape.
claims.why: The parsers in this chunk (_classify_failure, _parse_comment, read_pr_thread) either return explicit error statuses on malformed JSON or are tolerant of shapes; no silent 'absent' case is apparent.

observations.what: The docstring for screen_egress claims the returned rule is never matched text, but the evidence-path scan passes the actual path to secret_floor_rule. If secret_floor_rule returns its first argument on a match, the path would be leaked in the rule.

publish_to_pr and read_pr_thread both run the egress gate before checking for a PR reference, so a missing PR with a secret in the body will be refused as SECRET rather than PR_NOT_FOUND. This is likely intentional but could mask configuration errors.
load_for_publish reconstructs 'vendors_answered' using 'or answered', which could include vendors not in requested if the transcript is inconsistent. This is a fallback but may mask data issues.
read_pr_thread parses comments with _parse_comment but does not validate that each parsed turn is well-formed; a malformed comment could produce a PRTurn with missing fields.
